… Your Majesty’s sagely decree reads: “Those who govern All under Heaven must carefully consider what they esteem. The Xia esteemed wholehearted sincerity, the Yin simplicity, and the Zhou cultural refinement. These were all policies by which the sages remedied abuses. Toward the end of the Zhou, refinement increasingly predominated. Even during the flourishing Han, it was already said that Zhou refinement should be reduced and Xia sincerity put into practice. How much more necessary is it now, when we are ever farther removed from antiquity, to remedy the abuses of refinement! Yet human inclinations tend toward falsity just as water flows downward. If we now wish to reduce refinement and employ sincerity, by what path can this be achieved?”
That Your Majesty should speak of this is a blessing for the altars of soil and grain and good fortune for all your subjects throughout the realm. The moral condition of the age declines and flourishes; customs rise and fall. Yet the mainspring of these changes always lies in what the ruler esteems. In governing All under Heaven, the sages necessarily considered carefully what to esteem, thereby unifying what the people heard and saw and providing a foundation upon which their descendants could rely. Thus, the sincerity of the Xia, the simplicity of the Shang, and the refinement of the Zhou should surely have been transmitted for ten thousand generations without abuse. At the outset, the sages exhausted their thought in establishing laws and institutions, examining the distant past and consulting the circumstances of their own times. Could they have failed to know that sincerity readily degenerates into rusticity, simplicity into devotion to spirits, and refinement into scribal formalism? Would they nevertheless have left later generations the task of making incessant alterations? Alas, this is the force of circumstances! Even the sages could do nothing about it. How these practices are redirected and adapted depends solely upon those who come afterward. Sincerity and simplicity are not two different things. An earlier Confucian scholar said: “With sincerity there is an undivided wholeness of honesty and earnestness; there is no separate simplicity to speak of.” Such was the government of high antiquity, which could have been maintained from generation to generation. The Zhou succeeded the two preceding dynasties; following their ways would likewise have sufficed to achieve good government. Why, then, was it necessary to embellish them with refinement? Yet when we examine the matter, Confucius said: “The Zhou looked to the two preceding dynasties. How splendid …

之矣非若末世之一于文利而巧文而不慚
者也文而至於勝焉孔子豈從之哉表記曰
周人近人而忠焉則周之所尚非一于文可
知也已判而為春秋分而為戰國文之弊也
極矣當漢盛時高帝除弊政孝文躬節儉其

漓識治之士懼其流而不可挽也時有董仲
===

之者也茲又損之者何蓋欲損其末世之所
趨而進之文質彬彬者也譬之暑謝寒代夏
葛冬裘天時人事自有不得不然者仲舒之

…“How splendid its cultural refinement!” It would thus seem that what Zhou esteemed was refinement alone. Yet the refinement Confucius praised should be understood as that of the earlier generations: refinement that attained the proper balance. His words “took the two preceding dynasties as its models” mean that Zhou already combined the wholehearted sincerity of Xia and the unadorned substance of Shang. It was unlike the final age, which devoted itself exclusively to outward refinement, pursuing advantage with cunning and displaying polish without shame. If refinement came to predominate over substance, how could Confucius have followed it? The Record of Exemplary Conduct states: “The people of Zhou were close to others and wholehearted toward them.” We can therefore see that what Zhou esteemed was not refinement alone. With the realm's division in the Spring and Autumn period and its fragmentation in the Warring States period, the abuses of refinement reached their extreme.

In the flourishing days of Han, Emperor Gao abolished harmful policies, and Emperor Xiaowen personally practiced frugality. Did these not approach the surviving legacy of wholehearted sincerity and unadorned substance? Yet elaborate formalities gradually proliferated, and the ancient Way grew weaker by the day. Men who understood good government feared that this current could not be reversed. At that time, Dong Zhongshu earnestly submitted his three policy essays, wishing to reduce Zhou's refinement and put Xia's wholehearted sincerity into practice. Now Zhou's refinement had itself made adjustments at a juncture when the accumulated abuses of successive kings had reached their extreme. Why diminish it yet again? The intention was to curb the tendencies of its final age and advance toward a harmonious balance of refinement and substance. It is like heat giving way to cold, with kudzu cloth worn in summer and fur in winter: the seasons of Heaven and the affairs of men naturally have changes that cannot be otherwise. Was Zhongshu's intention not precisely that of Confucius in choosing to follow the earlier generations?

Alas, the ruler of outstanding ability and grand strategy failed to discern the critical opportunity, while ministers such as Hongyang and Bu Shi likewise failed to promote the substance of these proposals. Men of official standing did not shrink from deception; officials and commoners joined one another in wrongdoing. Customs deteriorated, and in the end no one reversed their decline. From Tang and Song onward, matters grew still worse.

title: 嘉靖四十四年進士登科錄
text:
國家當革鼎之始際剥復之餘碩果不食真精
再完若一開闢然此文復為質之機也而我
太祖又以敦朴先之如床碎鏤金服御澣濯隙地
種蔬農家進食何其儉約之若此也當其時
天下化之文具省而實意多道德一而風俗
同所謂太和元氣之會未凋未琢之天也而
三代不足言矣
列聖相承重熈累洽而我
皇上又以渾厚培之
訓誥頻仍
===
詔旨諄切冗費裁革玩好不留忠也質也兼而
用之者也
聖明之好尚豈非一時之規畫乎凡我臣工涵育
於紀綱振作之中薫陶於
恭修玄默之治固宜黜囂浮之習而進之唐虞
之盛矣况一心所欲百體爭趨一人所命四
海向風焉有上之人所好在此反違其所令
也乃今觀之天下文極矣庶民之家競以奢
侈相尚而尊卑貴賤之無制冠昏喪祭之踰
度豈無如賈誼之言於漢文者乎禮失而采

punctuated: 國家當革鼎之始，際剥復之餘，碩果不食，真精再完，若一開闢然。此文復為質之機也。而我太祖又以敦朴先之，如床碎鏤金、服御澣濯、隙地種蔬、農家進食，何其儉約之若此也！當其時，天下化之，文具省而實意多，道德一而風俗同，所謂太和元氣之會，未凋未琢之天也，而三代不足言矣。列聖相承，重熈累洽，而我皇上又以渾厚培之。訓誥頻仍，詔旨諄切，冗費裁革，玩好不留，忠也、質也，兼而用之者也。聖明之好尚，豈非一時之規畫乎？凡我臣工，涵育於紀綱振作之中，薫陶於恭修玄默之治，固宜黜囂浮之習，而進之唐虞之盛矣。况一心所欲，百體爭趨；一人所命，四海向風。焉有上之人所好在此，反違其所令也？乃今觀之，天下文極矣。庶民之家，競以奢侈相尚，而尊卑貴賤之無制，冠昏喪祭之踰度，豈無如賈誼之言於漢文者乎？禮失而采
translation_en:
…our dynasty, at the beginning of its transformation and renewal, emerged from a time of stripping away and restoration. The great fruit remained uneaten, and its true vital essence became whole again, as though heaven and earth had been opened anew. This was the moment when refinement could return to substance. Our Taizu further led the way through earnest simplicity: smashing a bed ornamented with carved gold [?], having his garments washed, planting vegetables on unused ground, and accepting food presented by farming households. How frugal and restrained he was! At that time, all under Heaven were transformed by his example. Empty formalities diminished, while genuine intent abounded; moral principles were unified, and customs became shared. This was what is called a convergence of supreme harmony and primal vitality, a natural condition as yet uncarved and unworked. Even the Three Dynasties scarcely merited mention beside it.

Successive sage emperors inherited the throne, adding brilliance to brilliance and prosperity to prosperity. Our present Emperor has further nurtured this legacy through generous sincerity. His admonitions and proclamations have been frequent, his edicts earnest and emphatic. Superfluous expenditures have been curtailed or abolished, and objects of amusement and pleasure have not been retained. Sincerity and simplicity have thus both been put into practice. Are not the preferences of our sagacious sovereign a guiding pattern for the age?

All of us, his servants and officials, are nurtured amid the revitalization of governing principles and discipline, and imbued with the influence of a government marked by reverent cultivation and profound quietude. Surely we should discard habits of clamorous frivolity and advance toward the flourishing age of Tang and Yu. Moreover, whatever the single heart desires, all the body's members hasten to pursue; whatever the One Man commands, all within the Four Seas turn toward his influence. How could people instead disobey his commands when these are the preferences of their ruler?

Yet, looking at the present, outward refinement throughout the realm has reached an extreme. Commoner households compete in esteeming luxury and extravagance. Distinctions between superior and inferior, noble and base lack regulation, while cappings, weddings, funerals, and sacrifices exceed their proper bounds. Are there not conditions like those of which Jia Yi spoke to Emperor Wen of Han? Ritual loses its proper character and becomes mere ornament…

樂失而淫豈無如嚴安之言於漢武者乎好
文而益偷飾詐而相高豈無如蘇子之論於
宋時者乎風俗至此駸駸乎不如
國初之舊矣昔堯有天下而晉陽之民被其餘
俗千有餘年而蟋蟀所咏至今猶可想其憂
深思遠之風焉如此乎聖化之遠也今
聖人在上奚啻堯德而中外之民又其所親炙而
薰陶者乃其風俗大有異於蟋蟀焉豈聖人
之化能被於千萬世之後而不能加於一世
之近耶臣嘗深思其故矣盖唐之風所以萬
===
世稱淳者非堯之自為也忠信之長慈惠之
師有以體其德意而奉行之也如舜之温恭
如禹之勤儉其他教稼穡明人倫治山澤典
五禮司五刑所以經綸世道者又莫不有真
實之心以行於其間以實心建實業夫是以
觀其化者有時雍之美薰其德者有可封之
俗而渾渾噩噩至今為烈也已夏商周所尚
若循環然其初之所以政平俗美而詐偽不
生士朴民純而趨向有定亦非上之人自為
也有禹湯文武之君而又有禹湯文武之臣

translation_en: …Music has lost its proper bounds and become licentious: is there no one to speak as Yan An did to Emperor Wu of Han? People prize outward refinement yet grow ever more lax, embellishing their deceit and competing to outdo one another: is there no one to argue as Master Su did in Song times? Customs have reached such a state that they are steadily falling below the old standards of our dynasty’s founding. Formerly, Yao possessed all under Heaven, and the people of Jinyang continued to benefit from the customs he bequeathed for more than a thousand years. Even today, from what is sung in “The Cricket,” we can still imagine their disposition to feel deep concern and think far ahead. Such is the far-reaching influence of a sage’s transforming guidance! Now a sage reigns whose virtue is surely no less than Yao’s, and the people both at the center and beyond are personally exposed to his influence and nurtured by it. Yet their customs differ greatly from those depicted in “The Cricket.” Can a sage’s transforming influence reach thousands upon thousands of generations into the future, yet fail to extend to his own immediate age? Your servant has often pondered the reason deeply. The customs of Tang, Yao’s realm, have been praised for their purity through all ages not because Yao acted alone. Loyal and trustworthy leaders, kind and generous teachers, embodied his virtuous intentions and put them into practice. There were Shun’s gentleness and reverence, and Yu’s diligence and frugality. Others taught sowing and reaping, clarified human relationships, managed mountains and marshes, presided over the Five Rites, and administered the Five Punishments. All those who thus ordered the world’s affairs brought genuine sincerity to their work. With sincere hearts they established substantial achievements. Thus those who witnessed their transforming guidance saw the beauty of universal harmony, and those nurtured by their virtue acquired customs that made everyone worthy of enfeoffment. Their simple, unspoiled integrity remains an illustrious example even today. The values esteemed by Xia, Shang, and Zhou succeeded one another as though in a cycle. At the outset of each dynasty, government was equitable and customs admirable, deceit and falsehood did not arise, scholars were unassuming and the people pure, and their aspirations had a settled direction. This, too, was not accomplished by rulers acting alone. There were rulers such as Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and there were also ministers serving Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu…

translation_en:
…taking the lead at the outset and maintaining these practices thereafter: this is why the people of the Three Dynasties were transformed without difficulty. Thus the cause of present-day habits and preferences can readily be understood. Scholar-officials are models for the people. When Jun Chen reverently upheld the established standards, none failed to change; when honored guests possessed virtuous reputations, they showed the people how to avoid frivolity. The origins of good customs recorded in the Book of Odes and the Book of Documents may be compared to an upright gnomon casting a straight shadow: the principle necessarily holds true.
Your Majesty has repeatedly taken pains to issue edicts, yet the longstanding abuses arising from the predominance of outward refinement have still not been entirely corrected. Might this be because the responsible officials have failed to carry them out sincerely? Among those who guard the altars of soil and grain at court and those who disseminate imperial governance throughout the realm, there must surely be men who administer affairs with sincere hearts. Yet might there also be some who merely present an impressive spectacle, without accomplishing anything that secures the state? Among the censorial and remonstrance officials who submit proposals at court, and the grand coordinators and regional inspectors who investigate and impeach in the provinces, there must surely be men who offer counsel with sincere hearts. Yet might there also be some who merely craft skillful arguments, without contributing plans that remedy the troubles of the age? Among those entrusted with the people and their local altars, how could there be no conscientious and capable officials? Yet if some embellish their speech with pleasing words while lacking a heart that regards themselves and the people as one body, their professed love for the people is not necessarily genuine. Among those stationed where benefit and harm hang in the balance, how could there be no men of resolution and courage? Yet if some broadcast empty boasts while seldom showing the integrity to stand firm alone, their undertaking of responsibilities is not necessarily genuine. …these officials, in their capacity as exemplars for the people, truly fall short of the ministers of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. If no example is established, what can the people look to? Would it not be difficult to expect their customs to resemble those of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties? This is what troubles Your Majesty. Human inclinations tend toward falsity as water flows downward; firm embankments must therefore be provided to restrain them [?]. Your servant requests leave to present six measures for your consideration and selection.
First, curb advancement by undeserved good fortune. In the past, Zhang Shizhi said that if the Bailiff were promoted out of turn for his verbal dexterity, he feared that everyone under Heaven would bend before the prevailing wind. His purpose was to prize substance. Those who now obtain office through clever speech possess merely the outward forms and lack substance: how can the state rely on them? The prestige and authority of office must be carefully guarded. When examining officials reward and select men, they must ensure that none advances undeservedly; when the personnel authorities promote men, they must ensure that none obtains a position undeservedly; when Surveillance Commissioners recommend men, they must ensure that none receives an undeserved recommendation. Then those who pursue fame and seek official salaries may desist somewhat.
Second, esteem frugality and simplicity. In the past, when Zichan governed Zheng, he supported and allied himself with those dignitaries who were loyal and frugal, while taking action to bring down those who were extravagant and lavish. His purpose was to exemplify simplicity. Those who now flaunt and esteem wealth and rank merely squander resources without restraint: how will they sustain this afterward? Standing regulations must be established. Caps and robes must conform to prescribed styles, and those who exceed them must be punished; banquets must be held on proper occasions, and those who hold them at improper times must be demoted; gifts must accord with ritual propriety, and those who violate it must be dismissed. Then the fashion for artificial finery and excessive extravagance may diminish somewhat.
Third, scrutinize the accepted standards of public affairs. Encouragement and punishment depend upon the arguments and charges presented by remonstrance officials. If they ascertain the facts and report them to the throne, do they not provide the reliable service expected of its ears and eyes? Yet private interests in disparaging or praising others must not be indulged. …what the established practice in ordinary times has been [?]. If this is not grounded in fact, it is no true comprehensive scrutiny. Might there not be those who label even a Wei Liaoweng a false gentleman?
Fourth: exercise care in choosing the shepherds of the people. The integrity and restraint of prefects and magistrates bear directly upon moral influence and public customs. If truly suitable men are found and retained in office for a long time, what habits and customs could fail to be corrected? Yet greedy and base conduct must not be tolerated. When gifts of gold brought under cover of night circulate openly, where are the admonitions governing official conduct? Officials go on filling their private purses, knowing nothing of the people’s hidden sufferings. To tolerate this is not genuinely to care diligently for the people. Might there not be those who, unwilling to let one household weep, cause an entire circuit to weep?
Fifth: give weight to virtuous conduct. Schools are the gateway for worthy scholars. Today literary learning advances with flourishing refinement, yet many men of outstanding ability remain confined within the study of textual phrases, and many quiet, retiring scholars are overlooked in recommendation and recruitment. If recruitment did not depend exclusively on the civil-service examinations, but occasionally employed summonses and invitations, the realm’s true talents would emerge. Shudu’s magnanimity was like a vast ocean: those who met him spontaneously lost their baseness and miserliness. Could this not help restore public customs?
Sixth: bring discipline to officials close to the throne. The capital is the place that should lead in goodness. Today the many officials take one another as models, spreading their influence widely; yet many still use the name of quiet restraint to occupy their offices idly, or indulge partisan interests to secure their own convenience. If they truly ceased to rest content with expediency and strove to strengthen their reputation and integrity, models for the whole realm would be established. Yang Wan was pure and upright; all who heard of him reduced their mounted attendants and retinues. Could this not provide an opportunity to transform the moral condition of the age? All these are expedient measures for remedying abuses, and the ministers charged with carrying them out ought to give them practical effect. 雖然，所以勸臣者有本焉。昔者董子之告其君也，有曰：「正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民。」臣以是知群臣者，民之表也；臣心之誠偽，固民俗之所由以淳漓。大君者，臣之主也；君心之邪正，又臣工之所視以為則傚。其機捷於桴鼓，神於風草，不可不審也。

translation_en:
…Yet today even scholar-officials cannot act thus. Why is this?” Reading these words, your servant wonders: is it only Your Majesty who doubts this? Your servant too is perplexed. If one does good with some ulterior purpose, that goodness must lack sincerity; if one acts loyally only when prompted, that loyalty must fall short of completeness. Judging circumstances and responding to change are matters in which the initiative rests with those above; serving the public and upholding rectitude are responsibilities resting with those below. Anyone who would fulfill his responsibilities yet still waits for rewards or intimidation is no loyal minister. To recover the loyalty and simplicity of the Xia and Shang and establish principles to be upheld unchanged for all ages depends simply on officials themselves making these qualities real.
Nevertheless, there is a foundation for encouraging ministers. Master Dong once advised his ruler: “Rectify your heart to rectify the court; rectify the court to rectify the hundred officials; rectify the hundred officials to rectify the myriad people.” From this your servant understands that ministers are models for the people: the sincerity or falsity of ministers’ hearts determines whether popular customs are wholesome or debased. The sovereign is the master of his ministers: the crookedness or rectitude of his heart likewise provides the example that officials look to and imitate. This influence works more swiftly than a drum responds to its stick, more wondrously than grass responds to the wind. It must be carefully considered.
Your servant reverently reflects that Your Majesty has composed an admonition on Reverent Single-mindedness and annotations on the Four Admonitions. Thus you have surely cultivated in advance, and steadfastly maintained, the Way of unceasing, perfect sincerity. A discussion of rectifying the heart would seem to have no need of my humble offering of celery and sunshine. Yet since Your Majesty began by making Master Dong’s words the subject of your question, your servant in turn presents Master Dong’s words to Your Majesty. Loyalty means being centered in the heart: it is undivided purity, making no distinction between what is hidden and manifest, or between this and that.…

translation_en: When ministers serve their ruler with loyalty, extending it to the subtlest thought and the most manifest deed, with not the slightest thing that cannot be made known to their ruler, official standards of conduct will be rigorously observed, and those who serve as models for the people will be upright. When Your Majesty conducts yourself with wholehearted sincerity, extending it to the deepest palace chambers and to reverent attendance in the ancestral temple, with not the slightest thing that cannot be made known to Heaven, the sovereign’s ultimate standard will be established, and a complete model will be provided for all officials. We shall then see the court leading the hundred officials, and the hundred officials leading the myriad people, all encouraging one another toward loyalty and generosity. Even those who harbor deceit and selfish designs or vie in extravagance and luxury will all say: “What does the sagely Son of Heaven esteem? What do the worthy dukes and ministers uphold? How, then, could we dare to persist in mean and ungenerous conduct?” Manners will be honest and customs admirable; people will act without being ordered and desist without being forbidden. Officials will be free of treachery and wrongdoing, and the people will not overstep their proper bounds. Virtue will nourish even the grasses and trees, and its transforming influence will reach beyond the realm. Such flourishing could equal that of Tang and Yu—the ages of Yao and Shun. Why, then, need the Three Dynasties even be mentioned? Your servant’s reckless and unseeing words, the humble views of a grass cutter and wood gatherer, take no account of what must not be spoken. I am overcome with trembling fear, apprehensive in the extreme of falling into ruin.
